title: Lentils: protein, fiber, iron, and calories

seo.title: Lentils: protein, fiber, iron, and calories
seo.meta_description: Cooked lentils: ~116 calories, 9 g protein, 7.9 g fiber, and 3.3 mg iron/100 g. One cooked cup provides nearly 18 g protein.
seo.search_intent: Understand cooked lentil nutrition and why dry values cannot be compared directly with cooked values.

excerpt: Cooked lentils provide about 116 calories, 9 g protein, 7.9 g fiber, and 3.3 mg iron per 100 g. A cooked cup provides nearly 18 g protein and 16 g fiber. Dry values are much higher per 100 g because the lentils have not absorbed water yet.
content_html:
Lentils are a perfect example of why nutrition numbers need a preparation state. One hundred grams dry and 100 g cooked do not represent the same amount of original lentil solids. Cooking adds water, so nutrients become less concentrated per 100 g.

Cooked lentils: what reaches the plate

Per 3.5 oz (100 g) cookedApproximate amount
Calories116 kcal
Protein9.0 g
Carbohydrate20.1 g
Fiber7.9 g
Fat0.4 g
Iron3.3 mg
Folate~180 mcg

One cooked cup is about 198 g, which works out to roughly 230 calories, 17.8 g protein, 15.6 g fiber, and about 6.6 mg iron.

Dry vs. cooked: ~24–25 g vs. ~9 g protein per 100 g

Dry lentils contain about 24–25 g protein and roughly 350 calories per 100 g, compared with 9 g protein and 116 calories when cooked. Cooking did not destroy two-thirds of the protein; water greatly increased the weight.

That is why comparing 100 g dry with 100 g cooked compares different amounts of dry matter. Use the value that matches the food as you actually eat it.

Protein matters, but fiber changes the comparison

One cooked cup provides almost 18 g of protein. The same 198 g of cooked chicken breast would provide more than 60 g protein, but the lentils also provide about 15.6 g fiber while chicken provides 0 g.

They are different nutrient profiles, not gram-for-gram substitutes.

Lentils are rich in iron, but it is nonheme iron

At roughly 3.3 mg per 100 g cooked, lentils contribute a meaningful amount of iron. It is nonheme iron, which is absorbed more variably than heme iron from meat.

Eating lentils with vitamin C-rich foods—such as bell pepper, tomatoes, citrus, or kiwi—can improve nonheme iron absorption.

Fiber is one of their biggest strengths

A cooked cup provides about 15–16 g of fiber. That fiber adds bulk to the meal and reaches the colon, where some of it is fermented by gut microbes.

Canned lentils live in the “cooked” world

Canned lentils are already hydrated and cooked, so their protein and calorie values per 100 g are much closer to boiled lentils than dry lentils. Sodium is the bigger variable; check the drained weight and Nutrition Facts label.

You do not have to pair lentils with rice at the same meal

Lentils contain all essential amino acids, but their amino-acid pattern differs from egg, meat, and dairy proteins. That quality distinction does not change the roughly 9 g protein per 3.5 oz (100 g) in cooked lentils; a varied diet supplies other amino acids across the day, so a legume and grain do not have to be eaten in the same bowl.

Bottom line

For a real meal, cooked values are the useful reference: about 116 calories, 9 g protein, and 7.9 g fiber per 100 g. A cooked cup provides nearly 18 g protein and 16 g fiber, plus iron and folate.

faq.question: How much protein is in cooked lentils?
faq.answer: About 9 g per 3.5 oz (100 g); one cooked cup provides nearly 18 g.

faq.question: How much fiber is in lentils?
faq.answer: Cooked lentils provide about 7.9 g fiber per 100 g, or roughly 15–16 g per cooked cup.

faq.question: Why do dry lentils have more protein per 100 g?
faq.answer: Because they have not absorbed cooking water. After boiling, the same nutrients are distributed across a much larger food weight.

faq.question: Is the iron in lentils well absorbed?
faq.answer: It is nonheme iron, which is variably absorbed. Eating lentils with a vitamin C source can improve absorption.
